Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the model forecasts compared to true outcomes.

Looking at the data patterns:

## Example 1 (2024-11-25)
- History: Price started around 65.47 and gradually increased to 69.27
- Model forecasts: Start at 69.70, gradually decaying to 75.29
- True outcomes: Start at 69.86, gradually decaying to 72.17

The model is consistently forecasting about 0.3-0.6 units higher than true outcomes for the first 15 days. Looking at the decay pattern - the model's 30-day forecast is slightly too high compared to reality.

## Example 2 (2024-11-22)
- Very similar to Example 1, just 3 days earlier
- Model forecasts start at 69.09 vs true 69.27 (under by ~0.18)
- But by day 15+, model is again slightly too high

## Example 3 (2024-11-26)
- History includes the final 69.86 price point
- Model forecasts: 69.33 → 67.13 (decrease of 2.20)
- True outcomes: 69.23 → 73.46 (decrease of 4.23)

Wait, let me look more carefully. The model is forecasting more deceleration in the decline than actually happens. The model thinks prices will keep falling more quickly, but they flatten out and decline less than modeled.

## Example 4 (2024-11-21)
- History starts at 66.40 (slightly different from 65.47)
- Model forecasts: 69.88 → 75.09 (decrease of 5.21)
- True outcomes: 69.99 → 74.36 (decrease of 5.63)

The model under-forecasts the magnitude of the decline by about 0.4-0.6 on average.


The model consistently underestimates price movements, particularly in the early days, with a bias towards predicting more rapid declines than actually occur. Sentiment indicators of 0.67 or higher correlate with increased prediction errors, suggesting complexity in translating market sentiment into accurate price forecasts.

Analyzing the divergence between model predictions and true outcomes reveals a systematic underestimation of price movements, especially in the initial 15-day projection period. The model tends to forecast more gradual declines than reality demonstrates,
